scenes.title: What the connection allows

beats.text: A taut, inextensible rope fixes the separation. Along a straight road, both bodies therefore share an acceleration.
Light means negligible mass. Accelerating the rope needs no resultant force, so its end tensions are equal.
A rope pulls each body towards the other. It can carry tension, but cannot push.
Consider a braking car and a trailer with negligible resistance. A rigid tow bar pushes the trailer backwards, slowing it: thrust, or compression.
With a rope, the trailer approaches the car. The rope goes slack: zero tension, and acceleration need not be shared.

scenes.title: Picture the towing journey

beats.text: Consider a car towing a trailer along a straight, level road, joined by a light rigid tow bar.
Driving force exceeds resistance, so both vehicles speed up together.
Find their common acceleration and tow-bar tension. Here is the complete question.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The car has mass eight hundred kilograms.
The trailer has mass two hundred kilograms.
The engine provides a constant fifteen hundred newtons to the right.
Constant resistance on the car is three hundred newtons to the left.
Constant resistance on the trailer is two hundred newtons to the left.
The road is straight and level. Model both vehicles as particles and the tow bar as light and inextensible.
Find their common acceleration, a, and the tension, T, in the tow bar.

scenes.title: Choose which body to study

beats.text: Right is positive. Weight and normal reaction balance vertically; consider horizontal forces.
On the trailer, tension pulls right and resistance acts left. Engine force acts only on the car.
On the car, tension and resistance act left; driving force acts right.
Start with Newton’s law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Enclose both vehicles. The connection forces are internal: equal and opposite.
Adding forces cancels plus T with minus T. They remain on individual vehicles, but vanish from the combined equation.
With shared acceleration, the system mass is the sum of both masses.

scenes.title: Find the common acceleration

beats.text: For the whole system, resultant force equals total mass times acceleration.
Driving force minus both resistances equals the sum of the masses times a.
Substitute fifteen hundred for the driving force.
Subtract three hundred for car resistance.
Subtract two hundred for trailer resistance.
The car contributes eight hundred kilograms.
Add two hundred kilograms for the trailer, then multiply by a.
The resultant is one thousand newtons and the total mass is one thousand kilograms.
Divide both sides by the total mass.
The acceleration is one metre per second squared, to the right.
Both gain the same velocity each second, keeping the separation fixed.

scenes.title: Find the tension using the trailer

beats.text: To find tension, isolate the trailer. Its force equation contains T; the whole-system equation does not.
Start again: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Tension minus trailer resistance equals trailer mass times the shared acceleration.
Subtract the trailer’s two hundred newtons of resistance from T.
Use its mass of two hundred kilograms.
Multiply by the acceleration, one metre per second squared.
Add the resistance to both sides. Tension supplies the resultant and overcomes the resistance.
The tension is four hundred newtons.
That force pulls the trailer right and the car left. Equal forces do not mean equal resultants, because each vehicle has other forces.
Check the car separately: driving force minus resistance minus tension equals car mass times acceleration.
Fifteen hundred, minus three hundred, minus four hundred, equals eight hundred times one. Both sides agree.

scenes.title: Check your understanding

beats.text: Can we cancel tension when studying the trailer alone? Take a moment.
No. The opposite tension acts on the car, outside the trailer’s boundary.
Increase trailer resistance, keeping engine force and masses unchanged. The smaller forward resultant means smaller acceleration.
Explain a shared acceleration.
